story_ideas.title: Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2027
story_ideas.headline: The wage figure inside the COLA notice is doing more work than the raise
story_ideas.angle: A short explainer on the $72,800.33 national average wage index for 2025 named in the 10/26/26 notice and the program parameters the notice says it sets, for people still working past 65 and anyone claiming soon.
story_ideas.hook: Coverage of the 3.6 percent increase almost never mentions the second number in the same document, which the notice says also drives other program parameters.
story_ideas.summary: Under title II of the Social Security Act (Act), there will be a 3.6 percent cost-of-living increase in Social Security benefits effective December 2026. In addition, the national average wage index for 2025 is $72,800.33. The cost-of-living increase and national average wage index affect other program parameters as described below.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are still earning, pull your Social Security earnings record and read it against the wage index figure in this notice rather than against last year's headline percentage.
story_ideas.b2b: Advisers and benefits counselors fielding December questions need the determination notice itself, not the press summary, because the parameters clients ask about are in the body of it.
story_ideas.chart: The underlying file supports an original ranking or trend line.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: Someone deciding when to claim is making that decision against the parameters in this notice, and the announced percentage alone does not tell them what changed.
story_ideas.note: National figure, no state cut, but it reaches every beneficiary household and lands squarely in open enrollment season.

story_ideas.title: Medicare Program; Implementation of Sections 6219, 6220, and 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
story_ideas.headline: A proposed rule would force Medicare plans to keep their doctor lists accurate
story_ideas.angle: A walk through the three sections in the 10/20/26 proposed rule, Part D cost-sharing reductions for low-income individuals, the REAL Health Providers Act provider-directory requirements, and pharmacy benefit manager accountability, for beneficiaries choosing a plan right now.
story_ideas.hook: The rule is still proposed, which means the directory and cost-sharing provisions are open to comment rather than settled.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you pick a plan, call two doctors listed in its directory and confirm they take it; this rule exists because those lists have been wrong.
story_ideas.b2b: Plans and pharmacy intermediaries should be reading section 6224 now, since accountability requirements written at the proposed stage are cheaper to shape than to retrofit.
story_ideas.why: Choosing a plan from an inaccurate directory can leave you paying out of network for a physician you believed was covered.
story_ideas.note: No monitored publisher matched this item, a confirmed gap, and the proposed status gives it a live deadline.

story_ideas.headline: Every Medicare-registered home health agency near you, with its ratings attached
story_ideas.angle: A how-to built on the refreshed 09/21/26 file listing all Medicare-registered home health agencies with addresses, phone numbers and quality measure ratings, for families planning a hospital discharge.
story_ideas.hook: The agency a discharge planner suggests is usually the only one a family hears about, and this file lists all of them with ratings.
story_ideas.summary: A list of all Home Health Agencies that have been registered with Medicare. The list includes addresses, phone numbers, and quality measure ratings for each agency.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask the discharge planner for three agency names, then look up each one's quality ratings in this file before you agree to any of them.
story_ideas.b2b: Agencies competing on ratings in a county where families can now see the full list should know where they sit against every neighbor, not just the ones they lose referrals to.
story_ideas.localize: Breaks down to US states, US counties — rank the outliers.
story_ideas.competitive: One or two monitored publishers have touched it.
story_ideas.why: Picking the agency that was handed to you, rather than the best-rated one serving your zip code, shapes months of care at home.
story_ideas.note: Localizable to states and counties; only light coverage found among monitored publishers.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Home Health Care - Patient Survey (HHCAHPS) State Data 2025Q2 to 2026Q1
story_ideas.headline: What home health patients in your state actually said about their care
story_ideas.angle: A state-by-state read of the HHCAHPS patient survey file covering 2025Q2 to 2026Q1, for readers comparing home care in the state they live in to the state a parent lives in.
story_ideas.hook: Patient survey results are the one home health measure that comes from patients rather than from claims, and the state file makes them comparable.

story_ideas.b2b: Operators in states that trail the national averages will be answering for the gap in referral conversations once anyone charts it.

story_ideas.title: Medicaid Estate Recovery: State Strategies to Mitigate Harm
story_ideas.headline: After Medicaid pays for a nursing home, the state can come after the house
story_ideas.angle: An explainer on the 10/20/26 Justice in Aging analysis of how states can reduce the harm of Medicaid estate recovery, for low-income older adults and heirs who do not know recovery exists.
story_ideas.hook: Estate recovery is a rule families usually meet after a death, when nothing can be done about it.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask your state Medicaid agency in writing what it recovers and what hardship waivers it grants, before an application rather than after a funeral.
story_ideas.b2b: Facilities and their admissions staff field recovery questions constantly and mostly guess; state-level variation is the part worth briefing.
story_ideas.why: A family that learns about recovery too late can lose the one asset it expected to inherit.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap among monitored publishers, and the state-strategy framing makes it localizable to any single state.

story_ideas.headline: The Medicaid payments that decide what a nursing home can afford to staff

story_ideas.hook: State directed payments are the quiet mechanism moving large sums into nursing home rates, and the brief looks specifically at the nursing home slice.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are comparing facilities in two states, the money reaching each one differs by state policy, not by how good the building looks.
story_ideas.b2b: Operators and investors modeling state exposure need the nursing-home-specific cut of directed payments rather than the aggregate Medicaid picture.
story_ideas.why: The payment structure behind a facility is part of whether it can hold staff through the year you need it.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap; pairs naturally with state Medicaid fact sheets for a two-state comparison.

story_ideas.hook: States have not settled how they will verify the medical frailty exclusion, and the brief looks to SNAP's history for what that process tends to look like.

story_ideas.b2b: Providers who complete verification paperwork for residents and clients should plan for the administrative load before states finalize their processes.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** A 3.6 percent cost-of-living increase in Social Security benefits takes effect in December 2026, set out in the Federal Register notice published 10/26/26 that also gives the national average wage index for 2025 as $72,800.33 and states that both figures set other program parameters. The raise arrives in the same month that a proposed rule published 10/20/26 would implement section 6219 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, adjusting Medicare Part D cost-sharing reductions for low-income individuals, and in the same month Justice in Aging published its 10/20/26 analysis of what states can still recover from the estates of people whose care Medicaid paid for. Read together, these three make it possible to answer a question an announced percentage cannot: what the December increase is worth to a beneficiary whose drug costs and benefit eligibility are tested against income. These are separate documents from separate bodies, not one story arriving three ways.

**Why it matters:** The 3.6 percent is the same for every beneficiary. What it does to the rest of a household's year is not. The notice itself says the increase and the wage index drive other program parameters, and the 10/20/26 proposed rule would change how Part D cost-sharing reductions are calculated for low-income individuals, which is the same population for whom a few dollars of additional monthly income is consequential. The estate recovery analysis names the other end of the same ledger: what a state can take back after death from an older adult who was poor enough to qualify for Medicaid. A reader who only sees the percentage cannot tell whether their own net position improves in December.

**Why pitch this now:** The increase is effective December 2026 and the determining notice published 10/26/26. The Part D proposed rule published 10/20/26 is still at the proposed stage, which means comment is open and the final numbers are not fixed. KFF's 10/21/26 midterm fact sheet notes federal Medicaid eligibility and financing changes from the 2025 reconciliation law, including work requirements, are still ahead. A December-effective number explained in November is useful; explained in January it is history.

**Angle:** Whether the 2027 cost-of-living increase is still an increase once the other determinations the same notice triggers are applied to a low-income Medicare beneficiary. Working title: "What 3.6 Percent Is Worth in December." For older adults on fixed income and the adult children who handle their paperwork.

- **MarketWatch Retirement** — the $72,800.33 wage index figure and the benefit increase together are the kind of federal number its readers track against their own earnings record.
- **Provider Magazine** — its Medicaid and state-by-state readership will want the eligibility-threshold consequence for residents whose income is tested each year.

pitch_ideas_raw:
**The wage figure inside the COLA notice is doing more work than the raise**
*Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2027*  
- Angle: A short explainer on the $72,800.33 national average wage index for 2025 named in the 10/26/26 notice and the program parameters the notice says it sets, for people still working past 65 and anyone claiming soon.
- Hook: Coverage of the 3.6 percent increase almost never mentions the second number in the same document, which the notice says also drives other program parameters.
- For readers: If you are still earning, pull your Social Security earnings record and read it against the wage index figure in this notice rather than against last year's headline percentage.
- For the trade: Advisers and benefits counselors fielding December questions need the determination notice itself, not the press summary, because the parameters clients ask about are in the body of it.
- Why it matters: Someone deciding when to claim is making that decision against the parameters in this notice, and the announced percentage alone does not tell them what changed.
- Also: National figure, no state cut, but it reaches every beneficiary household and lands squarely in open enrollment season.
- Pitch to: Bankrate Retirement, ThinkAdvisor

**A proposed rule would force Medicare plans to keep their doctor lists accurate**
*Medicare Program; Implementation of Sections 6219, 6220, and 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026*  
- Angle: A walk through the three sections in the 10/20/26 proposed rule, Part D cost-sharing reductions for low-income individuals, the REAL Health Providers Act provider-directory requirements, and pharmacy benefit manager accountability, for beneficiaries choosing a plan right now.
- Hook: The rule is still proposed, which means the directory and cost-sharing provisions are open to comment rather than settled.
- For readers: Before you pick a plan, call two doctors listed in its directory and confirm they take it; this rule exists because those lists have been wrong.
- For the trade: Plans and pharmacy intermediaries should be reading section 6224 now, since accountability requirements written at the proposed stage are cheaper to shape than to retrofit.
- Why it matters: Choosing a plan from an inaccurate directory can leave you paying out of network for a physician you believed was covered.
- Also: No monitored publisher matched this item, a confirmed gap, and the proposed status gives it a live deadline.
- Pitch to: Fierce Healthcare, SeniorLiving.org

**Every Medicare-registered home health agency near you, with its ratings attached**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Home Health Care Agencies*  
- Angle: A how-to built on the refreshed 09/21/26 file listing all Medicare-registered home health agencies with addresses, phone numbers and quality measure ratings, for families planning a hospital discharge.
- Hook: The agency a discharge planner suggests is usually the only one a family hears about, and this file lists all of them with ratings.
- For readers: Ask the discharge planner for three agency names, then look up each one's quality ratings in this file before you agree to any of them.
- For the trade: Agencies competing on ratings in a county where families can now see the full list should know where they sit against every neighbor, not just the ones they lose referrals to.
- Why it matters: Picking the agency that was handed to you, rather than the best-rated one serving your zip code, shapes months of care at home.
- Also: Localizable to states and counties; only light coverage found among monitored publishers.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement

**What home health patients in your state actually said about their care**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Home Health Care - Patient Survey (HHCAHPS) State Data 2025Q2 to 2026Q1*  
- Angle: A state-by-state read of the HHCAHPS patient survey file covering 2025Q2 to 2026Q1, for readers comparing home care in the state they live in to the state a parent lives in.
- Hook: Patient survey results are the one home health measure that comes from patients rather than from claims, and the state file makes them comparable.
- For readers: Compare your state's patient survey scores to the national file before you accept the line that home care quality is the same everywhere.
- For the trade: Operators in states that trail the national averages will be answering for the gap in referral conversations once anyone charts it.
- Why it matters: Knowing your state runs below the national average changes which questions you ask an agency on the first call.
- Also: This is a refreshed public data file rather than an event, but it supports a clean fifty-state chart.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Long-Term Care News, Family Caregiver Alliance

**After Medicaid pays for a nursing home, the state can come after the house**
*Medicaid Estate Recovery: State Strategies to Mitigate Harm*  
- Angle: An explainer on the 10/20/26 Justice in Aging analysis of how states can reduce the harm of Medicaid estate recovery, for low-income older adults and heirs who do not know recovery exists.
- Hook: Estate recovery is a rule families usually meet after a death, when nothing can be done about it.
- For readers: Ask your state Medicaid agency in writing what it recovers and what hardship waivers it grants, before an application rather than after a funeral.
- For the trade: Facilities and their admissions staff field recovery questions constantly and mostly guess; state-level variation is the part worth briefing.
- Why it matters: A family that learns about recovery too late can lose the one asset it expected to inherit.
- Also: Confirmed gap among monitored publishers, and the state-strategy framing makes it localizable to any single state.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement

**The Medicaid payments that decide what a nursing home can afford to staff**
*A Closer Look at State Directed Payments for Nursing Home Services*  
- Angle: An unpacking of the 10/21/26 KFF issue brief on state directed payments for nursing home services, for readers who want to know why facility finances differ so sharply by state.
- Hook: State directed payments are the quiet mechanism moving large sums into nursing home rates, and the brief looks specifically at the nursing home slice.
- For readers: If you are comparing facilities in two states, the money reaching each one differs by state policy, not by how good the building looks.
- For the trade: Operators and investors modeling state exposure need the nursing-home-specific cut of directed payments rather than the aggregate Medicaid picture.
- Why it matters: The payment structure behind a facility is part of whether it can hold staff through the year you need it.
- Also: Confirmed gap; pairs naturally with state Medicaid fact sheets for a two-state comparison.
- Pitch to: Skilled Nursing News, McKnight's Long-Term Care News

**Proving you are too frail to work may come down to a form**
*Assessing Ability to Work: How Historical SNAP Processes May Vary from Medicaid*  
- Angle: A plain reading of the 10/22/26 KFF brief on how SNAP has handled verification challenges and what that suggests for the Medicaid medical frailty exclusion, for older adults who could be asked to document an inability to work.
- Hook: States have not settled how they will verify the medical frailty exclusion, and the brief looks to SNAP's history for what that process tends to look like.
- For readers: Start keeping copies of the medical documentation that shows what you cannot do, because an exclusion you qualify for still has to be proven on paper.
- For the trade: Providers who complete verification paperwork for residents and clients should plan for the administrative load before states finalize their processes.
- Why it matters: An exemption you qualify for but cannot document is the same as no exemption at all.
- Also: Highest-scoring confirmed gap in the run at 77, and it sits across nutrition, Medicaid and frailty at once.
- Pitch to: Fierce Healthcare, SeniorLiving.org

**Medicaid work requirements are coming and most enrollees have not been told how**
*Midterm Election Update: Medicaid Changes*  
- Angle: A reader-facing summary of the 10/21/26 KFF fact sheet on what the 2025 reconciliation law has already changed in Medicaid eligibility and financing and what is still ahead, for enrollees and their families.
- Hook: The fact sheet separates what has already taken effect from what is still pending, which is the distinction enrollees most often get wrong.
- For readers: Find out whether your coverage category is touched by the new work requirements and what your state has published about them so far.
- For the trade: Enrollment and eligibility teams can use the changed-versus-pending split to decide where to spend outreach effort before the requirements bite.
- Why it matters: Losing coverage to a requirement you did not know applied to you is the most preventable kind of loss in this file.
- Also: Only light coverage found; a state-level version is the obvious localization.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement

**What state Medicaid choices do to the paychecks of the people who come to the house**
*How Do Medicaid Policies for Home- and Community-Based Services Impact the Jobs and Wages of the Formal Care Workforce?*  
- Angle: A report on the 10/20/26 Center for Retirement Research study linking Medicaid home- and community-based services policy to jobs and wages in the formal care workforce, for families relying on paid aides.
- Hook: Aide turnover is usually explained as a labor market problem, and this study points at state Medicaid policy instead.
- For readers: When an agency cannot keep an aide on your parent's schedule, ask what the state pays for that service; the answer is often the reason.
- For the trade: Home care operators arguing for rate increases now have a research citation tying state HCBS policy directly to wages and employment.
- Why it matters: Continuity of the person who shows up at the door is the part of home care families feel most, and it tracks a policy they can see.
- Also: Confirmed gap; the study's state-policy framing invites a comparison between two neighboring states.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Home Care, SeniorLiving.org

**The Medicaid contracts almost nobody can read**
*Reporting and Transparency Requirements for State Medicaid Agency Contracts (SMACs)*  
- Angle: An accountability piece on the 10/21/26 Justice in Aging explainer covering reporting and transparency requirements for State Medicaid Agency Contracts, for beneficiaries who want to know what their state promised a contractor.
- Hook: Oversight of these contracts is the mechanism standing between a beneficiary and a contractor's performance, and the requirements are not widely understood.
- For readers: If a managed care plan denies you a service, ask your state Medicaid agency what its contract requires the plan to report about denials.
- For the trade: Contractors and state agencies facing stronger reporting expectations should know which disclosures are already required before an advocate asks for them.
- Why it matters: A denial you cannot trace to a contract term is a denial you cannot appeal effectively.
- Also: Confirmed gap and fully state-by-state; one state's contract makes the whole story concrete.
- Pitch to: Fierce Healthcare, SeniorLiving.org

**How much of your state is on Medicaid, in one page**
*Medicaid State Fact Sheets*  
- Angle: A guide to using the 10/19/26 KFF state fact sheets, which give coverage, access and financing data plus a politics section for every state, for readers trying to judge their own state's exposure.
- Hook: The sheets put coverage, financing and state politics on the same page, which is unusual and makes comparison fast.
- For readers: Pull the fact sheet for your state and the state your parent lives in and compare the coverage share before any move or care decision.
- For the trade: Operators planning multi-state expansion can use the financing and politics sections as a first screen on state risk.
- Why it matters: Your state's Medicaid position determines what your family can count on, and most people have never seen the figure.
- Also: Confirmed gap; fifty-state structure makes it the easiest localization in the run.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement
